newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian PM says socialist scandal not hurting govt.
newsitem.headline: Belgian PM says socialist scandal not hurting govt.

text.p: Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene, whose coalition faces a vote of no-confidence over bribes allegedly paid to one of the partners, said the scandal had no impact on the government's ability to rule.

Shrugging off reports of tensions in the four-party coalition and calls for the Francophone Socialist Party (PS) to leave the government, Dehaene said there are "no direct problems" at the heart of his centre-left coalition.

In an interview in Belgium's L'Echo newspaper published on Friday Dehaene, a Flemish Christian Democrat (CVP), also appeared to rule out early elections, reiterating that the government's term ran until 1999.

Last week two former senior officials of the PS were arrested and later charged with corruption in connection with an investigation of a 1989 bribes-for-airforce-contracts affair implicating French defence firm Dassault.
Their lawyers have said that on behalf of the PS the officials, both aides to senior party politicians, received 30 million francs (about $1 million) from Dassault.
Dassault has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing.
A former Belgian army colonel, reportedly a lobbyist for Dassault, has also been charged with corruption.
Legal moves to start questioning a previous leader of the PS party are under way.
The no-confidence vote requested by the opposition will be held next week. The government is expected to win,
In vintage Dehaene style the Prime Minister brushed aside suggestions the scandal would split the coalition wide open and bring down the government.
Asked about the reliability of the PS party as a coalition partner and calls by the opposition PRL liberal party to change the coalition, he said firmly: "I have a government agreement."
"If there is quarrelling between the parties, let them resolve that between themselves. I see no repercussions (or) direct problems at the heart of the government," he added.
"I have a government programme for which I need the whole of the political term of office (until 1999)."
Dehaene is eager to complete preparations for Belgium to join Europe's Economic and Monetary Union, due to start in 1999, without having to change his team of ministers.

Newspaper commentators have already in the past accused the prime minister of being obsessed about joining the currency union, autocratically holding the reins of government and ensuring power does not slip away before the task is finished.
They suspect Dehaene has been working behind the scenes this week to limit the fallout of the scandal.
The allegations made in the Dassault affair "do not interfere at all in the way policy is carried out and the way the parties work today," Dehaene said.

He noted that, before a 1989 law, there had been problems with party financing for all parties because some money gifts had been seen as legal provided no favours were demanded in return and there had been "grey areas".
